title: Stop Trying to Read Your Leader’s Preferences
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership field note argues that good team members should stop guessing what their leader wants and instead initiate an explicit conversation about expectations. Because leaders are highly idiosyncratic, it treats mind reading as a losing proposition, and it recommends revisiting expectations periodically even in established relationships. The note identifies four topics that belong in that conversation: how success is measured, where the leader is headed, who decides what, and how to communicate. It explains the payoff of each, from avoiding effort spent on low-priority work to preventing leaders from feeling blindsided and team members from feeling micromanaged. The piece closes by urging readers who lack clarity to ask for it now and keep asking.
points: Leaders differ so much in their expectations that guessing them is described as a losing proposition.
The most important topic is how the leader defines success and judges performance in the role.
Understanding the leader's long-range goals and upward pressures lets team members make sensible day-to-day trade-offs.
Explicit decision rights prevent the misunderstandings that do the most damage in reporting relationships.
Communication preferences should cover update frequency, format, detail, and which problems require immediate escalation.
quotes: Attempting to guess what the leader above you wants from you is a losing proposition. As a rule, leaders are highly idiosyncratic in what they expect from those who report to them.
The better course is to take ownership of an explicit conversation about expectations as early in the relationship as possible.
Four topics deserve a place in the conversation: how success is measured, where the leader is headed, who decides what, and how to communicate.
Clarity prevents the all-too-common problem where a team member works hard on things the leader values far less than the team member assumed.
When these boundaries are made explicit, leaders avoid feeling blindsided, and team members avoid feeling micromanaged.
Reading minds is a guessing game. The best team members don’t presume to know what is on the leader’s mind. They simply ask for a preview, achieve clarity, and keep asking.
